**W6: About generalisation and evaluation.**

We agree that our terminology should more carefully separate adaptability from strict zero-shot generalization and that our claims should stay within what the data supports.

> Rephrasing claims.

We revised the text in $\S$4.3–4.4 and in the $\S$5 Discussion to use "rapid adaptation" and "data/time efficiency" when describing fine-tuning on new subjects, and avoid phrasing that could be read as implying fully zero-shot generalization. To our knowledge, no existing model achieves strong zero-shot image reconstruction on NSD; we explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation.

> On subject diversity.

NSD indeed trades breadth of subjects for depth per subject. While we currently do not include results on broader-cohort datasets (such as HCP 7T movies) due to computational constraints, our framework is agnostic to the particular ROI mask and registration procedure and can in principle be applied to other tasks (including auditory and motor paradigms). We toned it down in $\S$5 Discussion, suggesting that we have not already demonstrated this and instead present it as an important direction for future validation.

> Qualifying the cohort-scaling statement.

In $\S$4.4 we state that models without strong anatomical priors may treat increasing subject variability as noise. We agree that, taken literally, this attribution can be confounded by other differences between architectures. We will soften this sentence to:
"Under our experimental setting, models that ignore anatomy experience a larger drop in CLIP performance when the training cohort expands from 4 to 8 subjects (e.g., SIM `[1]`: −2.0 points vs NeurIPS: −0.6; Fig. 5 Right), suggesting that anatomy-conditioned routing may improve robustness to cohort scaling."

**W7: About using image reconstruction as an evaluation metric.**

We strongly agree with this broader concern and appreciate the suggestion.

- *Existing semantic evaluation: brain captioning*. In addition to reconstruction, we already evaluate NeurIPS on brain captioning following UMBRAE (Xia et al., 2025) `[16]`. Table 4 (in Appendix) and Figure 10 (in Appendix) show that our model substantially outperforms Yu et al. `[2]` and SIM `[1]` on a suite of captioning metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, CIDEr, SPICE, CLIP-S), and generalizes across subjects. We will make this more visible by briefly mentioning it in $\S$4.1 and pointing to Appendix E.
- *New retrieval metrics*. In response to your suggestion, we are adding a CLIP-space image retrieval evaluation: using the predicted CLIP image embeddings to retrieve the true stimulus from the test gallery, reporting brain-to-image retrieval Acc@1 of 91.1%, significantly outperforming SIM `[1]` (82.9%) and Yu et al. `[2]` (68.9%). (Table 7 in Appendix).  This directly probes representational alignment and bypasses the generative prior.

We believe that combining reconstruction, captioning, and retrieval provides a more balanced picture of the encoder’s quality and we will adjust the narrative accordingly.

### Questions

**Q1: Why does the model restrict computation to the visual cortex, when visual representations may also rely on distributed activity across parietal, temporal, and frontal areas?**

Because NSD is a static-image dataset, most stimulus-locked variance lies in occipital and ventral visual areas. Prior NSD decoders (e.g., MindEye `[13]`, MindBridge `[14]`, Yu et al. `[2]`) likewise restrict analyses to visual cortex for image-based tasks, and we follow this convention to stay comparable. Under a fixed compute budget, allocating dense spherical convolutions to the entire cortex forces us to shrink the network and harms performance. Our new full-cortex ablation confirms this: despite higher memory usage, it underperforms the visual-ROI SRST (Table 2, row #6). We will clarify this task-specific trade-off and emphasize that NeurIPS can in principle operate on other ROI masks for non-visual datasets.

We want to emphasize that this is a task-specific design choice rather than a claim that full-cortex modelling is inherently "wrong": in fact, SIM's `[1]` full-brain design is well motivated for its original audio–visual movie-watching setting, where distributed networks outside visual cortex are expected to contribute. In our NSD static-image setting, however, concentrating surface modelling in visual ROIs is a deliberate trade-off under fixed compute that yields better performance. We will clarify this trade-off in the revision and emphasize that NeurIPS can in principle operate on other ROI masks for non-visual or multimodal datasets.

### Questions

**Q1: The paper introduces the Conditional Information Bottleneck (C-IB) objective as theoretical motivation, but the connection to the implemented modules (SRST and SG-MoE) is not clearly explained. Could the authors elaborate on how these components operationalize the C-IB framework?**

As summarized above, SRST implements the "information-preserving" term by restricting encoding to a geometry-aligned visual ROI and preserving local neighborhoods, while SG-MoE implements the "identity-suppressing" term by conditioning computation on anatomy rather than subject ID. The empirical predictions derived from this C-IB view (efficiency, fast adaptation, robustness, anatomy usage) are all supported by our experiments. We will revise $\S$3 to spell out this mapping from the C-IB objective to SRST and SG-MoE more explicitly. 

**Q2: Figure 6A is described as showing that expert selection depends strongly on cortical origin but weakly on subject identity, yet the procedure for quantifying these dependencies is unclear. Could the authors explain how these dependence measures were computed and how to interpret the maps?**

As detailed in Appendix C, for each token and transformer layer we record the activated experts across all subjects and test samples. We then compute the variance of expert activations across brain regions (to measure region dependence) and across subjects (to measure subject dependence), ignoring [CLS] and [global] where appropriate. Bright regions in the left panel of Fig. 6A indicate locations where routing decisions vary strongly across regions (high region dependence); bright regions in the right panel indicate strong subject dependence. We observe that (i) region dependence is high in shallow layers and decreases with depth, and (ii) subject dependence is low for [CLS] tokens in deeper layers but intentionally retained in [global] tokens, which supports our design where [CLS] tokens become subject-invariant while [global] tokens carry subject-specific information.

### References

1. Wang, Shizun, et al. "Mindbridge: A cross-subject brain decoding framework." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2024.
2. Yu, Sijin, et al. "From Flat to Round: Redefining Brain Decoding with Surface-Based fMRI and Cortex Structure." *arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.16389* (2025).

**Q2: Does the model require pre-alignment across subjects (e.g., spherical registration to fsaverage), or is the anatomy-conditioned routing sufficient to handle inter-subject geometry?**

Yes. All NSD data are mapped to fsaverage6 using the standard FreeSurfer spherical registration provided in the NSD preprocessing pipeline. This is the same alignment strategy used in prior NSD decoding work `[2,13,14]`, so our model operates in the same common cortical space. We do not view this as a major limitation: these pipelines are widely used, and the cost of running them once per subject is small compared to model training. We stated this explicitly in the revision in $\S$3.2.

**Q3: How many fMRI frames as used as input?**

We use one GLM-estimated beta volume per stimulus image, registered to the cortical surface and masked by the ROI. This beta-based representation is standard for NSD image decoding (e.g., MindEye `[13]`, MindBridge `[14]`, Yu et al. `[2]`), and we adopt the same convention for comparability. There is no temporal sequence modelling in this work; each sample corresponds to one stimulus. Temporal information is integrated in the GLM step (over multiple TRs), and we leave explicit modelling of fine-grained dynamics (e.g., continuous movies) to future work.

**Q4: How is the model building a "topology-preserving space suitable for joint training." , this is not clear?**

SRST applies spherical convolutions on ROI-restricted surfaces, preserving local neighborhoods and sulcal topology during downsampling from *fsaverage6* to *fsaverage3* (Fig. 3). The resulting local and global tokens thus encode responses in a coordinate system that is already aligned across subjects via surface registration, making it suitable for cross-subject transformers. We've revised the manuscript $\S$3.4.

**Q5: Are ROIs subject-specific or common across all participants? If fixed, how does inter-subject variability in cortical folding affect performance?**

We use a common ROI definition (NSD-General mask) in fsaverage space, so the set of vertices is fixed across subjects after registration. Inter-subject variability in cortical folding is handled by the registration itself; SG-MoE then models residual differences in how anatomy (thickness, sulcal depth, etc.) modulates function on this common template. We will clarify this two-stage handling (registration + anatomy-conditioned routing) in $\S$3.2.

**Q6: Could the authors clarify what spherical operation is used? The paper strongly argues that flattening fMRI signals into 1D vectors discards geometric information and undermines cortical topology preservation. However, the perception decoder in the proposed framework (fMRI$\to$VAE latent) appears to do exactly that: it flattens ROI-masked fMRI signals following MindEye (Scotti et al., 2023).**

Following Yu et al. `[2]`, SRST utilizes spherical convolution blocks implemented based on SphericalUNet `[3]` (*fsaverage6*$\to$*fsaverage3* for activity and *fsaverage6*$\to$*fsaverage1* for structural channels) (Appendix D). The perception decoder indeed flattens ROI-masked fMRI into a 1D vector, but this branch is only a low-level auxiliary path; our geometric claims concern the semantic path. We will explicitly separate these design choices  in $\S$3 to avoid confusion.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their positive feedback and detailed summary of our paper's strengths.

We are very encouraged that the reviewer found the paper clearly written and visually well-presented, noting the informative figures and extensive reconstruction examples. We are especially grateful for the recognition of our core contributions: that the anatomy-guided MoE is an "interesting and novel idea" for handling inter-subject variability, and that our experiments are extensive and demonstrate strong performance in reconstruction, adaptation, and efficiency.

We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the misleading wording in the legend of Figure 3, where SIM `[1]` was grouped under "spherical CNNs". This is our mistake in presentation, not a misunderstanding of SIM. SIM is not a spherical CNN but an icosahedral, patch-based surface transformer. In the revision we will (i) correct the Figure 3 legend to clearly distinguish spherical CNNs (e.g., Yu-style `[2]` sphere tokenizer) from patch-based methods such as SIM, and (ii) adjust the related-work paragraph to reflect this distinction.

To address the reviewers' constructive feedback regarding methodological rigor, baseline fairness, and evaluation scope, we have conducted extensive **new experiments** and added the following analyses:

1. Expanded Ablation Suite (Table 2): We implemented 7 new model variants to isolate specific design choices:

- Full-Cortex vs. Visual-ROI: We trained a full-hemisphere SRST variant to demonstrate that our ROI-restricted approach is not just more efficient (61GB vs 75GB memory), but also achieves higher semantic accuracy (93.2% vs 91.0% CLIP) under fixed resources (#6).
- Gating Signals: We compared anatomy-based routing against functional-feature gating (#7) and Yu-style `[2]` static structure fusion (#5), confirming that dynamic routing conditioned specifically on anatomical features provides the strongest inductive prior.
- Geometric Validity: To verify that our performance stems from actual geometric processing rather than simple feature pooling, we introduced local tokens drop (#8, #9),  position-shuffling (#10) and receptive-field restrictions (#11). The consistent performance drops in these settings confirm that exploiting cortical topology is essential for the model's success.

2. New Semantic Retrieval Benchmark (Table 7): To address concerns about the diffusion model dominating visual metrics, we added a Brain-to-Image retrieval task. NeurIPS achieves 91.1% Top-1 Accuracy, significantly outperforming SIM (82.9%) and Yu et al. (68.9%), proving superior representational alignment independent of the generative backend.

To assist the reviewers' reading, we have included here the **new experimental results** discussed in the rebuttal. The complete tables can be found in the revised manuscript.

---

**Table 2 (partial)**. Ablation studies on the NSD $\texttt{test}$ set providing causal evidence for our architectural design. Each row modifies a single component relative to the full model. Detailed analysis is provided in Section 4.5.

| #    | **Setting**               | Pixcor $\uparrow$ | SSIM $\uparrow$ | Alex(2) $\uparrow$ | Alex(5) $\uparrow$ | Incep $\uparrow$ | CLIP $\uparrow$ | Eff $\downarrow$ | SwAV $\downarrow$ |
| ---- | ------------------------- | ----------------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ | ---------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| 5    | Yu-style structure fusion | 0.239             | 0.359           | 89.7%              | 94.2%              | 90.9%            | 91.7%           | 0.669            | 0.412             |
| 12   | **Full Model**            | 0.248             | 0.370           | 90.7%              | 95.2%              | 92.3%            | 93.2%           | 0.663            | 0.404             |

**W4: Some worries regarding baseline comparisons and experimental fairness.**

We appreciate this and agree that these points need to be corrected and clarified.

> Correcting the SIM label.

You are absolutely right: SIM `[1]` is not a spherical CNN. It uses regular icosahedral tessellation and patch-level feature learning with a linear projection, whereas  SphericalUNet–style convolutions `[4]` in Yu-style sphere tokenizer `[2]` use hexagonal spherical convolutions. The confusion comes from a labeling mistake in Figure 3, where the "spherical CNN" icon was incorrectly annotated with SIM `[1]` instead of Yu et al. `[2]` This is a presentation error rather than a technical misunderstanding: in the main text and in Figure 7 we explicitly discuss how SIM differs from spherical CNNs and from our SRST. In the revision we will (i) correct the Figure 3 legend to attribute spherical convolutions to works such as Gu et al. and Yu et al., and (ii) describe SIM explicitly as an icosahedral, patch-based surface transformer.

> Clarifying training and inference parity.

As described in Appendix D/E, our re-implementations of SIM `[1]` and Yu et al. `[2]` use the official open-source code or the exact settings reported in their papers, and we align loss functions, data splits, optimization schedules, and the downstream diffusion backend with NeurIPS. For SIM specifically, we also scale its transformer to match our model's width and depth, which improves its performance; we report this stronger variant in Table 1. Appendix E details the image-reconstruction configuration, and Appendix F ("Comparison to Previous Work") explains that all main baselines in our figures (NeurIPS, MindBridge `[14]`, SIM `[1]`, Yu et al. `[2]`) share the same preprocessing and reconstruction pipeline, including the same Versatile Diffusion model and identical inference hyperparameters (number of steps, guidance scale, text–image mixup, etc.).

We add a short paragraph in $\S$4.1 explicitly summarizing these shared settings and pointing readers to Appendix E/F, to make the training and inference parity across methods more visible.

> About image reconstructions performance in Figure 1,4,5 and baselines training details.

We appreciate the suggestion to compare against methods explicitly designed for image reconstruction such as MindEye (Scotti et al., 2023) `[13]` and MinD-Vis (Chen et al., 2023) `[15]`. Our reconstruction figures actually cover two different scenarios, and this guided our baseline choice:

- *Full-data training* (Fig. 1, Fig. 4 right, Fig. 5). In this regime we aim to compare surface-based encoders under similar geometric assumptions. We therefore focus on SIM `[1]` and Yu et al. `[2]`, which, like our method, operate on cortical surfaces and implement geometry-aware tokenization. This allows us to isolate the effect of our ROI-restricted SRST and anatomy-conditioned SG-MoE from differences in voxel vs. surface representations or diffusion backbones. We will clarify this objective in $\S$4.1 and in the captions.
- *Resource-limited new-subject adaptation* (Fig. 4 left). Here, the focus is fast adaptation to unseen subjects under severe data/time constraints (20% data, 1 epoch). MindBridge `[14]` was specifically designed for this setting, with subject-specific parameters for rapid few-epoch adaptation, so it is the most appropriate baseline. In contrast, MindEye `[13]` and MinD-Vis `[15]` are optimized for per-subject training with larger budgets and do not directly address this constrained adaptation scenario. The "poor" image quality of MindBridge `[13]` and SIM `[1]` in Fig. 1 simply reflects this intentionally harsh fine-tuning regime; when training to convergence on all data (Fig. 4 right), all methods, including our re-implementations of SIM `[1]` and Yu et al. `[2]`, produce much higher-quality reconstructions.

To avoid any impression of unfairness, we (i) make these two regimes explicit in the main text and figure captions, and (iii) highlight that all reconstructions shown in the paper (NeurIPS, MindBridge `[14]`, SIM `[1]`, Yu et al. `[2]`) share the same Versatile Diffusion backend and identical inference hyperparameters, so differences in image quality stem from the fMRI encoding rather than from using different generative priors in $\S$4.1.

To assist the reviewers' reading, we have included here the **new experimental results** discussed in the rebuttal. The complete tables can be found in the revised manuscript.

---

summary.value:
Below are the main concerns from the reviewers and the rebuttal provided by the authors.

1. Conceptual positioning and novelty relative to prior surface-based work
Several reviewers (especially CyC1) argued that the paper overstates novelty by implying it “introduces” geometry-aware or surface-based decoding, while substantial prior work already exists. The concern was both about insufficient credit to prior literature and vague claims such as “inefficient surface tokenization.” The authors explicitly clarified that the contribution is not geometry-aware decoding per se, but how anatomy and geometry are operationalized (ROI-restricted surface tokenization + anatomy-conditioned MoE). They corrected mislabeling of prior methods, expanded related work, and refined claims.

2. Neuroscience grounding of visual-ROI restriction
A major concern was that restricting computation to visual ROIs is weakly justified neuroscientifically and appears driven mainly by computational convenience, ignoring distributed processing outside visual cortex. Reviewers requested empirical evidence that excluding non-visual cortex is not harmful. The authors added a full-cortex ablation under matched compute, showing worse performance and higher memory cost than the visual-ROI model. They clarified alignment with standard NSD practice and tempered claims to static image decoding.

3. Whether gains come from anatomy-aware routing or confounds (subject ID, generic MoE, learned convolutions)
Reviewers questioned whether improvements truly stem from anatomical priors rather than subject-ID leakage, generic MoE capacity, or learned spherical convolutions already present in prior work. The authors clarified that the main model uses structure-only gating (no subject ID), added explicit ablations for subject-ID gating, functional-feature gating, and Yu-style static fusion, and showed all underperform the proposed SG-MoE.

4. Ambiguity about geometric contribution vs. flattening operations
Concerns were raised that large parts of the pipeline still flatten fMRI into 1D vectors, potentially contradicting claims about preserving cortical geometry, and that global tokens dominate performance. The authors added geometry-sensitivity ablations showing consistent degradation, which supports genuine use of topology. However, the hybrid nature of the architecture (surface + 1D components) remains, and reviewers emphasizing strict geometric purity may still find this unresolved conceptually.

5. Evaluation dominated by diffusion-based image reconstruction
Multiple reviewers worried that reconstruction quality is dominated by the pretrained diffusion model, obscuring whether the fMRI encoder truly improves neural representations. They requested semantic-level evaluations. The authors added CLIP-space retrieval and brain-to-image semantic benchmarks, showing large gains over surface baselines independent of visual realism.

Among them, #2, #3, and #5 are fully addressed, but the remaining are partially addressed. Given the current ratings, I think the paper has not met the bar for acceptance.

comment.value:
**W2: There is little credit given to prior surface deep-learning approches or simply fair and correct mention of these works.**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We fully agree that there is a substantial body of work on surface-based deep learning and on modelling inter-subject variability, and that our current Related Work section does not give this literature enough visibility.

> Surface-based deep learning and cortical metrics.

Our intention was never to suggest that NeurIPS is the first to model fMRI or cortical metrics on surfaces. On the contrary, our work builds directly on previous surface convolution (Zhao et al., 2019/2021) `[3,4]` following Yu et al. (2025) `[2]`, and is inspired by transformer-based surface models (Dahan et al., 2022/2024/2025) `[1,5,6]`, all of which already account for cortical topology and geometry. We substantially expanded $\S$2 to (i) explicitly review these methods, (ii) clarify how they model fMRI and cortical metrics as signals on cortical manifolds, and (iii) position NeurIPS as advancing this line of work by how geometry and anatomy are operationalised, through a task-focused ROI surface tokenizer and anatomy-conditioned routing, rather than by introducing geometry-aware modelling per se.

> Inter-subject variability and registration.

We agree that inter-subject variability has been extensively studied from the perspective of anatomical and functional registration (e.g., Fischl, 2012 `[7]`; Robinson et al., 2014/2016 `[8,9]`; Glasser et al., 2016 `[10]`). Our experiments already rely on standard spherical registration to fsaverage from the NSD preprocessing pipeline, and NeurIPS is designed to sit on top of these well-validated methods, not to replace them. We revised $\S$2 and the $\S$5 to (i) explicitly reference these registration pipelines, (ii) clarify that they provide the initial topology-preserving common space, and (iii) explain that SG-MoE then models residual inter-subject variability by conditioning on cortical features instead of subject IDs. This should make clear that we appreciate inter-subject variability through both classical image-processing pipelines and feature learning, and that our contribution is to combine these perspectives.

> The real contribution lies in "how" geometry and anatomy are operationalised, not in introducing geometry-aware fMRI modelling per se.

We appreciate this assessment and largely agree with the way the reviewer articulates the contribution. Our goal is not to claim that NeurIPS is the first geometry-aware fMRI decoder. As the reviewer correctly notes, prior work such as Zhao et al. `[4]`, Gu et al. `[11]`, Dahan et al. (SIM) `[1]`, and Yu et al. `[2]` already model fMRI and cortical metrics as signals on cortical manifolds and explicitly account for topology and surface geometry. In the revision, we will make this much clearer by (i) expanding $\S$2 to more thoroughly review these surface-based approaches and (ii) explicitly stating that our contribution lies in how geometry and anatomy are operationalised through task-aligned ROI restriction and anatomy-conditioned routing, rather than in introducing geometry-aware modelling per se.

To support this re-positioning, we now provide ablations that isolate exactly these design choices while keeping the underlying surface machinery comparable to prior work:

- *ROI restriction vs full cortex*. A full-hemisphere SRST variant with the same spherical convolutions but no ROI restriction consumes more memory yet underperforms our visual-ROI SRST (Table 2, row #7), showing that geometry alone is not sufficient—the way tokens are allocated across cortex matters.
- *Anatomy-conditioned routing vs simpler structure fusion*. A Yu-style `[2]` structure-fusion variant that uses the same surface backbone but removes MoE routing yields a CLIP score of 91.7%, compared to 93.2% for our full SG-MoE (Table 2, row #7), indicating that the anatomy-guided routing mechanism itself is a key driver of the gain.
- *Structure vs subject ID vs functional gating*. Replacing cortical features with subject ID or simple functional descriptors in the gate consistently degrades performance relative to structure-only gating, reinforcing that which signal conditions computation is crucial.

We will also soften any phrasing in the $\S$1 and $\S$5 that could be read as overstating novelty, and we will highlight these ablations and the expanded related work to make it explicit that NeurIPS builds on existing geometry-aware decoders and aims to improve how geometry and anatomy are used, under matched training and inference settings, rather than competing by changing the evaluation protocol.

**Q7: Is there evidence of overfitting to the visual cortex when restricting ROIs?**

Our ROI-wise analyses (Fig. 6D,E) show that contributions are concentrated in known visual areas and follow the expected hierarchy rather than collapsing to a single parcel. The full-cortex ablation suggests that adding non-visual regions under fixed resources does not improve performance on NSD.

**Q8: Would the method still perform well if applied to non-visual fMRI datasets (e.g., auditory or motor)?**

For non-visual datasets, NeurIPS can ingest any binary ROI mask (e.g., auditory, motor, language networks); we will state this generality while clearly acknowledging that our experiments are currently limited to visual NSD.



### References

1. Dahan, Simon, et al. "SIM: Surface-based fMRI Analysis for Inter-Subject Multimodal Decoding from Movie-Watching Experiments." *The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations*. 2025.
2. Yu, Sijin, et al. "From Flat to Round: Redefining Brain Decoding with Surface-Based fMRI and Cortex Structure." *arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.16389* (2025).
3. Zhao, Fenqiang, et al. "Spherical U-Net on cortical surfaces: methods and applications." *International Conference on Information Processing in Medical Imaging*. Cham: Springer International Publishing, 2019.
4. Zhao, Fenqiang, et al. "Spherical deformable u-net: Application to cortical surface parcellation and development prediction." *IEEE transactions on medical imaging* 40.4 (2021): 1217-1228.
5. Dahan, Simon, et al. "Surface vision transformers: Attention-based modelling applied to cortical analysis." *International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning*. PMLR, 2022.
6. Dahan, Simon, et al. "Spatio-temporal encoding of brain dynamics with surface masked autoencoders." *arXiv preprint arXiv:2308.05474* (2023).
7. Fischl, Bruce. "FreeSurfer." *Neuroimage* 62.2 (2012): 774-781.
8. Robinson, Emma C., et al. "MSM: a new flexible framework for multimodal surface matching." *Neuroimage* 100 (2014): 414-426.
9. Robinson, Emma C., et al. "Multimodal surface matching with higher-order smoothness constraints." *Neuroimage* 167 (2018): 453-465.
10. Glasser, Matthew F., et al. "The human connectome project's neuroimaging approach." *Nature neuroscience* 19.9 (2016): 1175-1187.
11. Gu, Zijin, et al. "Decoding natural image stimuli from fMRI data with a surface-based convolutional network." *Medical Imaging with Deep Learning*. PMLR, 2024.
12. Allen, Emily J., et al. "A massive 7T fMRI dataset to bridge cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence." *Nature neuroscience* 25.1 (2022): 116-126.
13. Scotti, Paul, et al. "Reconstructing the mind's eye: fmri-to-image with contrastive learning and diffusion priors." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 36 (2023): 24705-24728.
14. Wang, Shizun, et al. "Mindbridge: A cross-subject brain decoding framework." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2024.
15. Chen, Zijiao, et al. "Seeing beyond the brain: Conditional diffusion model with sparse masked modeling for vision decoding." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2023.
16. Xia, Weihao, et al. "Umbrae: Unified multimodal brain decoding." *European Conference on Computer Vision*. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.

**W5: Some methodological clarifications are needed.**

> Role of the perception decoder.

We agree that the current phrasing can be misleading. The perception decoder is intentionally a standard 1D pathway, following MindEye `[13]`, and we do not claim any geometric innovation there. Our central geometric contribution lies in the SRST+SG-MoE semantic path. In fact, removing the perception decoder has a modest effect on semantic metrics but primarily hurts low-level visual fidelity (SSIM drops from 0.370 to 0.283, Table 2, row #3), consistent with its role as a detail-refinement branch. Meanwhile, removing the semantic branch causes a catastrophic collapse in CLIP score (93.2%$\to$55.0%, Table 2, row #4).

To make this distinction clearer and to ensure a fair comparison to surface-based baselines that do not use an additional perceptual head, we (i) explicitly state in $\S$3.2 and the $\S$5 Discussion that we are not proposing a new geometric architecture for the perception path but simply reuse a standard 1D design as an auxiliary head, and (ii) add a "NeurIPS (semantic-only)" row to Table 1 corresponding to the ablation without the perception decoder (Table 2, row #3). Extending the perception path itself to surface representations is an exciting direction for future work but beyond our current compute budget.

> Local vs global tokens.

It is true that the global token contributes strongly to high-level metrics (Table 2, row #1). To quantify the importance of local tokens as well, we added left-only and right-only local-token ablations (Table 2, row #8,9). Preliminary results show that removing local tokens from either hemisphere leads to consistent drops across high-level metrics, confirming that they are not redundant. We will include these numbers and a brief analysis in $\S$4.5.

In addition, we include two further controls that directly probe the role of geometry in SRST:

- *a position-shuffled variant*, where spherical vertex positions are randomly permuted before the convolutions, which substantially degrades performance (Table 2, row #10); 
- *a reduced-receptive-field variant*, where SRST uses only a single convolutional layer with a minimal spherical receptive field, which also lowers CLIP and related metrics (Table 2, row #11).

Together, these ablations show that (i) local tokens from both hemispheres contribute meaningfully, and (ii) SRST's geometry-aware neighbourhood structure, not just the existence of a global token, which is critical for the observed performance gains. We will report these results and a brief analysis in $\S$4.5.

> Their is no mention on how many fMRI frames are used at training or inference time.

We apologize for the lack of clarity here. In this work we do not train on raw fMRI time series or on stacks of "frames". Instead, following the standard NSD preprocessing pipeline `[2,13,14]`, we use GLM-estimated beta weights for each stimulus:

For every image, a general linear model is fit to the corresponding fMRI time course, and a single beta map is estimated that summarizes the stimulus-locked response over multiple TRs (accounting for the hemodynamic response and nuisance regressors). This beta-based representation is standard in NSD image-decoding work (e.g., MindEye `[13]`, MindBridge `[14]`, Yu et al. `[2]`), and we adopt the same convention to ensure comparability with prior methods. This beta map is then projected to the cortical surface and fed into our model as one sample. Thus, training and inference both operate on one beta per stimulus, rather than on raw temporal sequences. In this sense, temporal information is already integrated in the GLM step, and we do not perform additional temporal feature extraction beyond that. We will clarify this in $\S$3.2 by explicitly stating that our inputs are GLM beta maps (one per stimulus) rather than raw time series, and we will add a short note in the $\S$5 Discussion that modelling fine-grained temporal dynamics (e.g., for continuous movie paradigms) is an important future extension beyond the current beta-based setting.

summary.value:
This paper addresses the important modelling question of surface-based fMRI decoding and proposes NeurIPS, a framework designed to incorporate anatomical priors into the task of image reconstruction from fMRI data. The model introduces two core components: 1. the Selective ROI Spherical Tokenizer (SRST), which enables efficient, geometry-preserving encoding by focusing computation on selected cortical ROIs; 2. the Structure-Guided Mixture of Experts (SG-MoE), which uses anatomical features (thickness, curvature, sulcal depth) to route tokens and suppress subject identity information. The architecture follows a dual-decoder approach: a perception decoder mapping fMRI to VAE latent space and a semantic decoder aligning fMRI to CLIP embeddings. Both paths guide a diffusion model to reconstruct images from brain activity. The model claims strong efficiency, faster convergence, and state-of-the-art results on the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), while maintaining biological plausibility and scalability to new subjects.

While the reported performance is impressive, scientific rigour and clarity in methodology should not be compromised for empirical gains. Sound experimental design and fair comparisons are equally essential for assessing true progress.

strengths.value:
The paper is clearly written and visually well-presented. The figures are very clearly detailed and informative. There are many image reconstruction presented throughout the papers. 

The introduction of an anatomy-guided MoE is an interesting and novel idea for addressing inter-subject variability.

The dual-decoder design (semantic and perceptual) is consistent with recent diffusion-based pipelines.

The experiments are extensive, with scalability experiments, and ablations. Many metrics are used to assess the visual reconstructions. 

The model demonstrates strong performance on the benchmarked tasks of image reconstruction and adaptation to unseen subjects and efficiency gains (fewer epochs, smaller data fraction).

weaknesses.value:
Despite the strong quantitative results on image reconstruction metrics, the paper is not yet ready for acceptance due to several scientific, methodological and conceptual limitations.

1. The paper is missing some conceptual and methodological clarity.

- The paper presents several approximations and inconsistencies, particularly in how it positions itself relative to prior surface-based deep learning work. The papers is positioned within the real of geometric deep learning and surface-based modelling while actually one-stream within the entire model (in the SRST) module is modelling signal directly over the surface (only the visual cortex), the rest of the fMRI stream flattening the data into a 1D vector. 

- The paper claimed computational advantage (>70% fewer tokens) which is not clearly demonstrated against the use of the entire cortical surface. Additionally the neuroscience motivations for this are not precisely detailed (see below) or compared to such choices in the rest of the literature. The term “inefficient surface tokenization” is quite vague; the paper should specify what it means and why this "inefficiency" should prevail on neuroscience grounded motivations (extracting information from the entire cortical surface in response to multimodal external stimuli). 

2. There is little credit given to prior surface deep-learning approches or simply fair and correct mention of these works. 

- The paper does not properly or sufficiently acknowledge prior surface-based approaches that have introduced methodologies to model cortical metrics and fMRI signals as signals defined over cortical manifolds (e.g., Zhao et al 2019, 2021; Gu et al., 2023; Dahan et al 2022, 2024, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 etc..). These works already account for cortical topology and geometry into decoding frameworks and the paper does not introduce the progress that has been made by such methods in the past (in particular in the related work section) which might seem scientifically unfair. 

- There is no other reference to the question of modelling "inter-subject variability" despite the large neuroimaging literature addressing this concern via anatomical or functional registrations (Fischl 2012, Robinson 2014, 2016, Glasser 2016). This question is only appreciated through the lenses of feature learning rather than well validated image processing pipelines. 

- Overall, the paper risks overstating novelty and unfair comparison with existing literature. The real contribution lies in "how" geometry and anatomy are operationalised (ROI restriction + anatomy-conditioned routing), not in introducing geometry-aware fMRI modelling per se.    

3. There is limited neuroscience grounding in the method. 

- The restriction to visual ROIs lacks neuroscientific justification and appears motivated mainly by computational constraints (“to avoid the O(T²) burden of full-hemisphere processing”). Describing full-hemisphere processing as “inefficient” is scientifically questionable: functional networks are distributed, and signals outside the visual cortex (auditory, parietal, or frontal areas) can still contribute to visual decoding. Empirical evidence (e.g., Glasser et al. 2016, Nature, Huth et al 2016) shows that audio-visual perception engages a distributed cortical network; including auditory, motor, language, and memory regions; contradicting the assumption that non-visual areas are irrelevant or detrimental.
    
- The paper does not test this assumption: no ablation demonstrates that excluding non-visual regions improves performance.
    
- The rationale for conditioning on anatomical features (thickness, curvature, sulcal depth) rather than functional measures is not clearly justified.

4. Some worries regarding baseline comparisons and experimental fairness

- The manuscript inaccurately places surface-based method such as SIM (Dahan et al., 2025) under the umbrella of spherical CNNs (legend of Figure 3) . Instead this method is not based on spherical convolutions such as other surface-based method (Zhao et al 2019, that is not even referenced and given credit in this work, despite the mentioning of spherical convolutions similar to the Spherical UNet model) but on regular icosahedral tessellation and patch-level feature learning. The authors appear to conflate tokenisation with hexagonal convolutions (as in Zhao et al 2019), suggesting some misunderstanding of prior surface methods.

- It seems curious that image reconstructions performance throughout the paper (Figure 1, 4, 5) are not benchmarked models explicitly designed for image reconstruction that such as MindEye (Scotti et al., 2023) or Mind-Vis (Chen et al., 2023). Instead, the authors focus on using MindBridge and SIM only, showing poor image quality in Figure 1 (but not in Figure 4), with the later not being optimised for image reconstruction, but audio-visual retrieval. This is misleading and not task-matched. It would be better for the paper to show performance against model actively designed for image reconstruction.

- It also remains unclear how baselines are trained or if pretrained diffusion models were reused or fine-tuned under comparable conditions. Particularly, surface-based models can be highly dependant on the surface representations (fsaverage or ico spaces with regular spacing) ; as well as pre-training for frame reconstruction (Dahan et al 2025) or stimuli alignment (audio and visual in movie watching experiment); very little information is provided regarding these points. A table detailing training setup, data representation space, pretraining, and dataset usage for each baseline would improve transparency.
    

5. Some methodological clarifications are needed
    
- The perception decoder flattens fMRI inputs into a 1D vector, contradicting the paper’s central claim about preserving cortical geometry.  The geometric contributions remain ambiguous compared to prior work (e.g., Zhao et al. 2019, Dahan et al., 2022), and ablations indicate that the global token contributes most strongly to performance, raising questions about how much the geometric components truly matter.

- Their is no mention on how many fMRI frames are used at training or inference time. This is a critical aspect of the spatio-temporal extraction of information from fMRI data. There is no mention of temporal feature extraction. 

6. About generalisation and evaluation

- The paper equates fine-tuning on held-out test subjects (Figure 5) with “cross-subject generalization.” This measures adaptability, not zero-shot generalisation. True generalisation should be evaluated without any fine-tuning on new subjects. If the model encodes anatomical priors effectively, it should generalise naturally. This is a major bottleneck at the moment. 
    
- Claims about generalisation should also be tempered given the limited number of subjects in NSD (high within-subject sampling, low inter-subject diversity). Is there any additional experiments on wider datasets (less densely sampled but with more subjects i.e. HCP 7T movie-watching). 

- Some claims in the results sections (Section 4.4 "This result is significant: it suggests that models without strong anatomical priors may treat increased subject variability as noise, leading to performance degradation." ) for instance, are weakly supported, because several confounding factors (data preprocessing, architecture, and training differences) are not controlled.

7. About using image reconstruction as an evaluation metric.

- The heavy reliance on image reconstruction as a primary evaluation makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of the fMRI encoder from that of the pretrained diffusion model. Since the diffusion model dominates visual realism, improvements may reflect the generative prior rather than better neural representation learning. More broadly, this reflects a concerning trend in the field, where reconstruction quality is often prioritised over representational interpretability. In my view, this direction risks obscuring the real scientific question: how well we model the brain’s representational structure beneath the visual fidelity of generated images.

- More meaningful evaluations for this kind of frameworks would include semantic-level benchmarks (e.g., retrieval, classification, similarity) that directly probe representational alignment. We would encourage the authors to benchmark their model on well-established semantically task such as image or video retrieval to convince readers about the performance of their fMRI encoding method.

questions.value:
-  Why does the model restrict computation to the visual cortex, when visual representations may also rely on distributed activity across parietal, temporal, and frontal areas?

- Does the model require pre-alignment across subjects (e.g., spherical registration to fsaverage), or is the anatomy-conditioned routing sufficient to handle inter-subject geometry?

- How many fMRI frames as used as input?

- How is the model building a "topology-preserving space suitable for joint training." , this is not clear? 

- Are ROIs subject-specific or common across all participants? If fixed, how does inter-subject variability in cortical folding affect performance?

- Could the authors clarify what spherical operation is used? The paper strongly argues that flattening fMRI signals into 1D vectors discards geometric information and undermines cortical topology preservation. However, the perception decoder in the proposed framework (fMRI → VAE latent) appears to do exactly that: it flattens ROI-masked fMRI signals following MindEye (Scotti et al., 2023).

- Is there evidence of overfitting to the visual cortex when restricting ROIs?

- Would the method still perform well if applied to non-visual fMRI datasets (e.g., auditory or motor)?

We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the "novel integration of anatomical priors", the strong quantitative results, and the ablation study demonstrating that performance gains are driven by the architectural design.

### Weakness

**W1: The "Conditional Information Bottleneck" formulation is introduced as a motivation, but there is no empirical analysis showing how the model approximates that objective or reduces subject-specific information.**

Thanks for raising the question. We will mention explicit mapping from C-IB to modules. In Appendix B we already formulate cross-subject decoding as maximizing $I(Z;Y|A_s)-\beta I(Z;\texttt{ID}|A_s)$. We will add two concrete sentences making the mapping explicit: SRST increases by preserving surface neighborhoods and removing non-visual regions, thereby concentrating information on task-relevant cortex; SG-MoE reduces $I(Z;\texttt{ID}|A_s)$ by using cortical features, rather than IDs, as the routing condition, which “explains away” anatomical variance instead of memorizing subjects.

**W2: The rationale for adopting a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) conditioned on cortical features is insufficiently justified.**

**& W3: The method achieves strong quantitative results but lacks a clear causal or theoretical bridge between the stated motivation (modeling anatomical variability) and the proposed architectural solution (SG-MoE).**

Prior cross-subject work such as MindBridge `[1]` shows that injecting subject-specific parameters (e.g., subject embeddings or adapters) can be beneficial but scales linearly with the number of subjects. MoE offers a natural way to capture conditional specialization while sharing experts across subjects. Our SG-MoE extends this idea by replacing ID-based routing with anatomy-based routing, which we argue is a more principled conditioning signal for cross-subject generalization. We will revise $\S$1 Introduction and $\S$3 to make this motivation explicit in the main text.

To separate "using anatomy at all" from "using MoE specifically", we add a new ablation where we adopt a Yu-style `[2]` structure fusion module instead of SG-MoE routing (Table 2, row #5). This variant still uses cortical features but no longer uses conditional expert selection; it consistently underperforms SG-MoE (CLIP: 91.7% vs 93.2%). Together with the subject-ID gating baseline (Table 2, row #2), this provides causal evidence that how anatomy is injected, via conditional routing rather than simple fusion or ID gating, which does matter for performance.

**W4: The presentation could be clearer and more guided.**

We appreciate this feedback and will improve the narrative around the architecture and analyses.

We will add a short "roadmap" paragraph at $\S$3 that walks through the information flow: SRST $\to$ SG-MoE transformer $\to$ dual decoders $\to$ diffusion, with clear references to Figures 2 and 3.

We will introduce the new analogy figure (Figure 8 in Appendix) depicting natural image ROIs vs SRST visual ROIs to intuitively explain why selective ROI tokenization is meaningful in brain decoding.

For Figure 6, we restructure the text in $\S$4.6 to explicitly guide the reader through panels A–E: (A) routing dependence on region vs subject, (B) feature attributions demonstrating use of all four structural cues, (C) parcellation comparison validating NSD-General, (D) hierarchy across ROIs, and (E) contribution maps.

comment.value:
**W3: There is limited neuroscience grounding in the method.**

We appreciate this challenge and agree that our neuroscience justification can be made stronger and more explicit.

> Task-aligned visual ROIs and prior evidence.

NSD `[12]` is a vision-centric dataset where stimuli are static natural images. A large body of work `[2,12-14]` shows that the bulk of stimulus-locked variance for such tasks is concentrated in occipital and ventral visual cortex. Our SRST therefore operates on the NSD-General visual ROI mask provided by the dataset authors (9,488 vertices in *fsaverage6*), which specifically targets visually responsive cortex. This design is consistent with much of the NSD decoding literature (Mindeye `[13]`, Mindbridge `[14]`, Yu et al. `[2]`), where analyses are typically restricted to visual areas for image-based tasks. By contrast, SIM's `[1]` full-cortex design is well motivated for its original audio-visual movie-watching setting, where distributed networks beyond visual cortex are expected to contribute. We will make this task-alignment clearer in $\S$3.2, discussion and explicitly reference our ROI-wise analyses in Figure 6D,E, where decoding performance improves along the visual hierarchy and contribution maps are concentrated in visual cortex.

> New full-cortex ablation.

To directly test the effect of including non-visual cortex, we implemented a full-hemisphere SRST variant that processes all cortical vertices. Under a matched training budget, this variant requires substantially more memory (74.79GB vs 61.50GB GPU RAM) and achieves lower high-level metrics (e.g., CLIP: 91.0% vs 93.2% for our visual-ROI SRST; Table 2, #6). We will add this ablation to $\S$4.5, demonstrating that naive full-cortex tokenization is not only heavier but also less effective under fixed resources in this NSD setting.

>Clarifying scope claims.

We do not claim that non-visual areas are irrelevant for all tasks, nor that visual cortex exhausts the "true" network for perception. We soften sentences ($\S$3 Method, $\S$5 Discussion) that could be read this way and rephrase our claims as: given a fixed compute budget and a vision-only dataset like NSD, concentrating surface modelling in visual ROIs is a deliberate trade-off that yields better performance than full-cortex tokenization, while full-cortex modelling may be preferable for multimodal paradigms such as the audio-visual movie experiments targeted by SIM.

> The rationale for conditioning on anatomical features rather than functional measures is not clearly justified.

We agree that our rationale for using anatomical features in the router needs to be stated more clearly, and we thank the reviewer for prompting us to do so. Our design choice is driven by the specific role of SG-MoE: it is meant to capture stable, subject-specific variability that modulates how functional responses are expressed, while leaving stimulus-driven variability to the main encoder.

Cortical features such as thickness, curvature, sulcal depth, and area are (i) invariant across stimuli and sessions, (ii) tightly linked to folding patterns and micro-structural differences across individuals, and (iii) well known to correlate with functional organization. They therefore provide a natural signal for deciding which experts should process a token in a cross-subject model. In contrast, functional responses themselves are highly stimulus-dependent; using them directly as gating inputs risks entangling subject identity with trial-by-trial variability and duplicating information that is already encoded in the fMRI activity path.

To test this design choice empirically, we added a new ablation in which the SG-MoE gate uses functional features instead of anatomical ones (we replace thickness, curvature, sulcal depth, and area with simple functional descriptors such as the mean response, standard deviation, interquartile range, and overall skewness). 

Under identical training budgets and exactly the same experimental setting, this variant remains competitive but does not surpass structure-based gating (e.g., CLIP: 92.7% vs 93.2% for structure-only). These results suggest that, at least in the NSD setting, anatomical features provide the most effective and stable conditioning signal for routing, while functional information is better handled within the encoder itself. We will explicitly describe this motivation in $\S$3.4 and report the new ablations results in Table 2 in the revised manuscript.

First, we would like to sincerely thank the Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs for their time and effort. We have carefully read all comments and provided detailed point‑by‑point responses under each reviewer. Below we highlight what the reviewers appreciated about our work and the main improvements we made in the revision.

### **Overview**

Our proposed work, NeurIRS, studies cross-subject fMRI-to-image decoding in a surface-based setting and asks how neuro‑anatomical structure can be used as an inductive prior for generalizable and efficient decoding.

We introduce two main components in this work:

1. **Selective ROI Spherical Tokenizer (SRST):** A geometry-preserving surface encoder that restricts spherical convolutions to a task-aligned visual ROI mask, yielding efficient, topology-aware tokens.
2. **Structure‑Guided Mixture of Experts (SG‑MoE):** A cross-subject transformer whose routing is conditioned only on cortical features (thickness, curvature, sulcal depth, area), not on subject IDs, aiming to model anatomical variability rather than memorize identities.

On the NSD benchmark, our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance among surface decoders, exceeds strong 1D baselines while using only 11.6% tokens, and adapts rapidly to new subjects with limited data.

### **What the reviewers liked**

The reviewers agree that using cortical anatomy as an inductive prior is both novel and promising, and that our method is technically solid.

- **Method & Idea:** "A solid conceptual and technical advance" (Reviewer Ny4o); "the introduction of an anatomy‑guided MoE is an interesting and novel idea" (Reviewer CyC1); "novel integration of anatomical priors" (Reviewer MZd2).
- **Experiments:** "Architecture is thoughtfully designed and empirically validated" (Ny4o); "experiments are extensive... strong performance" (CyC1); "ablation study justified that the performance gain is driven by the design" (MZd2).
- **Presentation:** "Clearly written and visually well‑presented" (CyC1); "achieved high‑quality reconstruction" (MZd2).

### **What we did in the revision**

Based on the reviews, we substantially strengthened the paper along five axes:

**1. More experiments & ablations (updated in Table 2)**

- **Full‑cortex vs. Visual‑ROI SRST:** As suggested by **Reviewer CyC1**, we added a full‑brain variant as an ablation. Under the same training budget, this variant consumes more memory (75GB vs 61GB) yet underperforms our visual‑ROI SRST (CLIP: 91.0% vs 93.2%). This suggests that **for static image decoding, naive whole-cortex tokenization dilutes the signal with task-irrelevant regions, making it a less effective use of compute than our focused ROI approach.**
- **How anatomy is injected:** As suggested by **Reviewer Ny4o and MZd2**, we compared our approach against:
  - A **Yu‑style structure‑fusion** variant (no MoE routing): CLIP 91.7%.
  - **Subject‑ID gating** and **Functional-feature gating** variants: CLIP 89.8% and 92.7%, respectively.
  - **Result:** All perform worse than our structure‑only SG‑MoE (93.2%), demonstrating that **both explicit ROI restriction and anatomy‑conditioned routing are crucial to the gains.**
- **Geometry checks in SRST:** As suggested by **Reviewer CyC1**, we performed experiments on **dropping hemispheric tokens, shuffling spherical positions, and shrinking receptive fields**. These systematically reduced performance (e.g., shuffling positions dropped CLIP to 91.5%), confirming that the model genuinely exploits cortical topology and geodesic relationships.

**2. More evaluation beyond reconstruction**

To ensure fair comparison, we highlight that our work along with all other main baselines (SIM, Yu et al., MindBridge) use the same NSD preprocessing, diffusion backend, and inference hyper‑parameters. Differences in image quality therefore stem from the fMRI encoders.

As suggested by Reviewer CyC1, we added additional semantic‑level metrics:

- **Brain captioning** (following UMBRAE), where our proposed method outperforms surface baselines.
- **A new CLIP‑space retrieval benchmark (Table 7):** Our semantic decoder achieves **91.1%** brain‑to‑image accuracy, substantially outperforming SIM (82.9%) and Yu et al. (68.9%). This proves our proposed method improves semantic alignment, not just visual sharpness.

**3. Clearer comparison to prior surface‑based work**

We expanded the related work to thoroughly discuss spherical CNNs and surface transformers (Zhao et al., Gu et al., Dahan/SIM, Yu et al.) and classical inter‑subject registration (Fischl, Robinson, Glasser).

We explicitly clarify that our contribution is not "introducing geometry‑aware decoding" but how geometry and anatomy are used: a task‑aligned visual‑ROI surface tokenizer (SRST) and an anatomy‑conditioned MoE (SG‑MoE) for cross‑subject generalization.

**4. Stronger neuroscience grounding of the visual‑ROI design**

Addressing **Reviewer CyC1**'s concern regarding the visual-ROI input, we clarified that this is a deliberate design choice consistent with standard NSD benchmarks (MindEye, MindBridge, Yu et al.). We substantiated this choice using the **full‑cortex ablation described above**, demonstrating that extending the model to the whole brain under fixed compute significantly increases cost while degrading performance. This confirms that concentrating capacity on the visual hierarchy is the optimal trade-off for static image decoding, although our framework remains flexible for non‑visual masks in future tasks.

**5. Clarification on Generalization:** 

We refined our language to distinguish **rapid adaptation under limited data** from **strict zero‑shot generalization**, in line with **Reviewer CyC1's** suggestion.

We hope this summary helps the Area Chair see that the revised paper directly and substantively addresses the main concerns through new ablations, stronger neuroscience grounding, and richer semantic evaluation.

---
Best regards,

Authors of ICLR 2026 Submission 174

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful summary and for recognizing the novel, impactful contributions of our SRST's multi-scale tokenization and our SG-MoE's anatomy-guided approach to cross-subject generalization.

### Weakness

**W1: The contribution of trainable spherical convolutions in SRST remains unclear.**

We appreciate this request for clarification. We would like to gently correct a misunderstanding in the premise of the question. To the best of our knowledge, prior surface decoders such as Yu et al. (2025) `[1]` and SIM (Dahan et al., 2025) `[2]` already use learned kernels or projections rather than fixed filters: Yu et al. employ a SphericalUNet-based `[3]` trainable spherical convolution architecture, and SIM uses a fixed icosahedral tessellation for patch selection combined with a learned linear projection inside each patch. In Figure 7 we describe SIM's "sphere patch selection" as unlearnable because the patch grid on the sphere is predefined and not adapted to the task; this concerns where patches are placed, not whether the patch encoder itself is trainable.

We also note that in Yu et al. `[1]`, even when parts of the network are frozen after pretraining, the corresponding convolutional kernels are still the result of learning, not hand-crafted fixed filters. Thus there is no "fixed-kernel" baseline in the sense of non-trainable, analytic kernels in these works.

Our goal is therefore not to re-establish that learnable convolutions are better than fixed ones, but to show that how we use them, through selective ROI tokenization and anatomy-conditioned routing, which leads to substantially better performance and scalability than prior surface encoders.

To address your concern more directly, we have added a new ablation in Table 2 (row #5) where we replace our SG-MoE routing with a Yu-style `[1]` structure fusion module while keeping the rest of the architecture unchanged. This variant uses the same spherical convolutions but no longer routes computation based on anatomical features. Under the same training budget, this Yu-style fusion model achieves a CLIP score of 91.7%, compared to 93.2% for our full SG-MoE (Table 2, row #5). This confirms that the main gain is not from introducing trainable convolutions per se (which prior work already has), but from the combination of (i) ROI-restricted geometric encoding and (ii) structure-guided routing that exploits anatomy more explicitly.

We will revise the supplementary material and the ablation section to emphasize this distinction.

**W2: Although anatomy-aware, SG-MoE still uses subject-ID information.**

We apologize for the confusion here. Our current implementation of SG-MoE is already a pure structure-only variant: the gating network does not take any subject-ID input or subject embedding. Concretely, for each token we construct a gating input consisting only of local cortical features (thickness, curvature, sulcal depth, and ROI/location descriptors), and all expert weights are shared across subjects. The MoE therefore conditions computation exclusively on cortical structure, not on who the subject is. We will revise the text to state this explicitly and avoid the impression that SG-MoE mixes anatomy with subject IDs.

We believe the confusion comes from an ablation reported in the original paper where we replace cortical features with subject ID in the gate (Table 2, "subject ID gating" row, #2). That condition was deliberately designed as a contrastive control to test whether ID-based routing can match structure-based routing. In that ablation, using subject ID as the sole gating signal performs clearly worse than our structure-only SG-MoE on cross-subject metrics. In the revision, we (i) emphasize that all reported "SG-MoE" results correspond to the structure-only setting, and (ii) clearly label the ID-gating configuration as a separate control variant, whose weaker performance supports our central claim that routing by cortical structure, rather than subject identity, which is the more scalable and anatomically grounded inductive bias.

### References

1. Yu, Sijin, et al. "From Flat to Round: Redefining Brain Decoding with Surface-Based fMRI and Cortex Structure." *arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.16389* (2025).
2. Dahan, Simon, et al. "SIM: Surface-based fMRI Analysis for Inter-Subject Multimodal Decoding from Movie-Watching Experiments." *The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations*. 2025.
3. Zhao, Fenqiang, et al. "Spherical U-Net on cortical surfaces: methods and applications." *International Conference on Information Processing in Medical Imaging*. Cham: Springer International Publishing, 2019.

summary.value:
This paper presents a framework for cross-subject fMRI-to-image decoding. It introduces two main innovations: the Selective ROI Spherical Tokenizer (SRST) for geometry-preserving spherical tokenization, and the Structure-Guided Mixture of Experts (SG-MoE), which conditions fMRI decoding on cortical features such as thickness and curvature. Evaluated on the NSD dataset, they achieve state-of-the-art performance among surface-based decoders, fast adaptation to new subjects.

This work provides a solid conceptual and technical advance in cross-subject fMRI-to-image decoding. The architecture is thoughtfully designed and empirically validated. Its most valuable aspect is using cortical structure for generalization, marking an important step for brain decoding to generalize to unseen subjects.

While some methodological components (e.g., learned convolutions) could be better analyzed, the core idea of using cortical structure—rather than identity—for cross-subject generalization is novel and impactful enough to merit acceptance.

2.  Use cortical structure to improve cross-subject generalization. The SG-MoE conditions fMRI decoding on cortical features such as thickness and curvature, rather than only condition on subject ID. Conditioning on cortical structure is strongly more generalizable across subjects, this is a novel and impactful idea.

* The rationale for adopting a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) conditioned on cortical features is insufficiently justified. While the paper argues that anatomy should guide computation, it is not clear why MoE routing is the most appropriate or necessary mechanism for achieving this.
* The method achieves strong quantitative results but lacks a clear causal or theoretical bridge between the stated motivation (modeling anatomical variability) and the proposed architectural solution (SG-MoE). The design appears empirically driven, as if a modern MoE framework was applied to this problem and happened to perform well, rather than derived from principled reasoning about anatomy-function relationships.
* The presentation could be clearer and more guided. While the paper is technically strong, its exposition is dense and at times difficult to follow. Key components such as the information flow through SRST and SG-MoE are not explained intuitively, and the motivation for the architecture is buried among theoretical framing. For example, Figure 6 aims to demonstrate neuroscientifically plausible representations but lacks sufficient guidance in the text; readers may struggle to connect its visualizations to specific claims about anatomical dependence or cross-subject alignment.

### Weakness

**W1: The paper is missing some conceptual and methodological clarity.**

> Hybrid, not fully surface-based.

We appreciate the reviewer's concern about how we position the method within surface-based and geometric deep learning work. Our intention is not to claim that every part of the model operates on the cortical surface. Instead, the geometric inductive prior is concentrated in the SRST module, which focuses on the visual cortex, while later components operate on a compact token/latent representation.

Concretely, in SRST we restrict ourselves to vertices within the visual cortex; non-visual cortex does not participate in SRST. On this subset of the surface, we apply spherical convolutions on the cortical mesh to aggregate neighborhood information and then form (i) local tokens by pooling within anatomically defined visual ROIs and (ii) a global token summarizing the entire visual field. These geometry-aware tokens are then fed into the semantic decoder, which is where all of our architectural contributions lie. The perceptual decoder, in contrast, is a standard 1D pathway closely following prior work: it takes an ROI-masked 1D vector and serves as an auxiliary branch that mainly improves low-level image quality (e.g., SSIM), without changing the conclusions about our semantic encoder. Ablation results in Table 1 "NeurIPS (w/o perception decoding)" row shows that even when we remove the perceptual decoder, NeurIPS still outperforms all surface-based baselines on the main semantic metrics.

We will explicitly describe NeurIPS as a hybrid architecture in the Introduction and Methodology: a surface-based encoder for visual ROIs, followed by a compact token/latent space (and an optional 1D perceptual head) for efficient cross-subject training.

> Making the token efficiency claim concrete.

The current text loosely says that SRST reduces the token budget by "over 70%". We agree that this is vague. We will replace this with precise numbers derived from Table 1 and our ROI statistics:

At *fsaverage6* resolution, prior work such as Yu et al. `[2]` processes 40,962 vertices per hemisphere (40,962$\times$2 = 81,924 total). Our SRST restricts computation to the NSD-General visual ROI mask with 9,488 vertices (4,613 left / 4,875 right), yielding an 88.4% reduction in surface points processed (81,924$\to$9,488).

Internally, SRST downsamples to an *fsaverage3* representation where a full-hemisphere model would have 642$\times$2 = 1,284 vertices, while our selective visual ROI path uses only 145 tokens (70 left, 75 right), an 88.7% reduction.

We will update $\S$3.4 and the caption of Figure 3 to report these exact reductions and drop the ">70%" phrasing. 

> Clarifying "inefficient surface tokenization".

In this NSD image-decoding setting, by "inefficient surface tokenization" we mean area-uniform hemisphere tokenization: allocating tokens uniformly across the entire cortical surface, including large non-visual regions, rather than concentrating them in task-relevant visual cortex. Under a fixed compute budget, this forces one either to reduce model capacity or to accept unstable training. We will define this term explicitly in Introduction and tie it to the Input size column of Table 1 and to our new full-cortex SRST ablation (Table 2, row #6), which under matched training budget uses significantly more memory (74.79GB vs 61.50GB) yet produces lower CLIP scores (91.0 vs 93.2).

To further support this point, we already include an ROI-parcellation comparison (Figure 12 in Appendix), where we replace the NSD-General visual mask with two standard whole-cortex atlases (HCP-MMP1.0 and Yeo-17) and re-run our tokenizer on their visual parcels. The results show that the NSD-General, task-aligned ROI basis consistently yields better reconstruction metrics than these generic anatomical atlases, confirming that a functionally defined visual ROI basis is more effective for NSD image reconstruction than more diffuse whole-cortex schemes. In the revision, we will move this result from the appendix into the main discussion of SRST and explicitly describe our approach as a visual-cortex–focused, ROI-restricted surface encoder, rather than suggesting that we model the entire cortical surface.
